name: Nose-to-mouth ratio

card.summary: A facial-proportion measure comparing mouth width with nose width, used in looksmaxxing to judge lower-face harmony and decide whether nose or lip work might balance the face.
card.note: A community measuring convention rather than a clinical standard.

quick.overview:
The nose-to-mouth ratio compares the width of the mouth with the width of the nose on a front-on photo. Looksmaxxing forums commonly treat a mouth roughly one and a half times as wide as the nose as the target, and talk about figures such as 1.3 or 1.55.

People use it as a quick check on whether the lower face looks balanced. A low number is read as a wide nose or narrow mouth, which is why it comes up in discussions of rhinoplasty, alar base reduction and lip or smile changes.
quick.how: Users take a straight-on, neutral-expression photo, mark the widest points of the mouth and of the nostrils (alar width), and divide mouth width by nose width. Posters then share the number, often alongside before-and-after photos following a procedure or weight change.
quick.risks: The ratio is a community convention and the measurement shifts with lens distortion, head angle and expression. Using it to decide on surgery carries the usual risks of any cosmetic operation, discussed with a qualified surgeon.

lead: The nose-to-mouth ratio is a frontal facial proportion that divides mouth width by nose (alar) width. In looksmaxxing communities it is one of several numbers used to judge facial harmony, and it is cited when people consider changes to the nose or lips.[1][2]

Forum posts treat a ratio around 1.5 as ideal. One looksmax.org member reported moving from about 1.3 to roughly 1.55 within months and described the result as ideal, while another poster who measured 1.21 described wanting nose surgery to widen the gap.[3][4] Posters in the second thread argued that the nose sits at the centre of the face and strongly influences overall harmony.[4]

Published research has analysed frontal facial proportions of celebrities with automated tools, comparing racial groups and proposing benchmarks for attractive faces, though those papers examine a broad set of measurements rather than establishing a target for this particular ratio.[5][6]

chain: Measure mouth width against nose width in a frontal photo
Identify a wide nose or narrow mouth
Consider nose, lip or smile changes to rebalance the lower face
angle.text: People use the ratio as a quick screening number for lower-face balance. A higher value is read as a narrower nose relative to the mouth, and users discuss rhinoplasty or related procedures as ways to move it.

paras: The ratio uses two horizontal distances on a front-facing photo: the width of the mouth between the corners of the lips and the width of the nose across the nostril wings. Dividing mouth width by nose width gives the ratio. Forum posts mention values of about 1.2 to 1.3 as low and about 1.5 to 1.55 as ideal.[3][4]

On looksmax.org the ratio appears in threads where members report their own numbers and discuss changes. One poster reported a rise from about 1.3 to about 1.55 over a few months.[3] Another thread titled around a ratio of 1.21 and a wish for rhinoplasty argued that a wide, bulbous nose strongly lowers perceived attractiveness, and replies debated how nose width interacts with ethnicity.[4]
Community reasoning links the ratio to rhinoplasty, alar base reduction and lip-width or smile changes, as ways to change one of the two numbers.

Researchers have used artificial-intelligence software to measure frontal facial patterns of female and male celebrities, comparing racial groups to propose aesthetic benchmarks.[5][6] These studies look at many facial measurements together, and they do not present a single validated nose-to-mouth target.
No studies found specific to the nose-to-mouth ratio as defined in looksmaxxing communities. Related work on frontal facial proportions of celebrities exists.[5][6]

lore.intro: Members of looksmax.org post personal ratios and discuss them as part of nose-focused assessments.[3][4]

claims.claim: A ratio near 1.5 is ideal and a low ratio hurts the whole face
claims.believers: Posters say a wide nose is the most noticeable central feature and that a ratio around 1.5 reflects good harmony.[3][4]
claims.experts: No published study has validated a specific nose-to-mouth target; celebrity-face analyses measure many proportions together.[5][6]

claims.claim: Nose surgery can improve the ratio
claims.believers: One member described needing rhinoplasty after measuring 1.21 and others weighed in on nose width.[4]
claims.experts: Rhinoplasty changes nasal dimensions by design; no study of this specific ratio as an outcome was found.
